question: Can a solvable lazy random-feature model jointly explain how test loss scales with gradient-descent time, model width, dataset size, and compute, including finite-resource corrections, data-reuse overfitting, and the limited value of ensembling?

key_findings.claim: The paper's strongest contribution is a joint dynamical mean-field theory for time, sample, and random-feature bottlenecks in one structured linear model.
key_findings.evidence: A teacher is expanded in covariance eigenfeatures, while the student learns a Gaussian random projection of those features. In the proportional M,N,P limit, the authors close four correlation functions and four response functions, solve the time-translation-invariant responses in Fourier space, and recover the fully trained static random-feature results at low frequency. The cavity derivation also explains why many non-Gaussian independent entry distributions should share the same limit under a central-limit condition.

key_findings.claim: For imposed power-law spectra, the model derives distinct time and finite-resource exponents and an asymmetric compute allocation.
key_findings.evidence: With lambda_k proportional to k^{-b} and lambda_k(w_k*)^2 proportional to k^{-a}, the paper obtains L_time proportional to t^{-(a-1)/b} and L_data,L_model proportional to P^{-m},N^{-m}, where m=min(a-1,2b). Approximating the joint loss by the sum of independent bottleneck terms and imposing C=Nt gives t proportional to C^{bm/(a-1+bm)}, N proportional to C^{(a-1)/(a-1+bm)}, and the corresponding optimal loss exponent. The result is clean but conditional on exact spectral tails and an additive bottleneck approximation rather than a theorem for a joint finite system.

anchors.section: N. Compute optimal scaling from sum of power laws

key_findings.claim: The theory gives a useful temporal account of finite-data overfitting, but only inside squared-loss linear dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: The train-test gap is expressed exactly through the response R_0,2 and the training correlation C_1. High-frequency expansion gives early O(1/P) corrections, while reused finite data can produce a nonzero late gap and double-descent-like width behavior. In contrast, the one-pass construction draws a fresh independent batch at every step and equates expected train and population loss, so it cannot represent persistent-example memorization, correlated streams, or distribution drift.

anchors.section: Gradual buildup of overfitting, Equation 18 and Figure 5
Figure 10 early stopping and double descent

key_findings.claim: The ensembling result is a conditional bias-variance statement, not a universal proof that going wider always dominates ensembling.
key_findings.evidence: The cross-system DMFT separates initialization and dataset variance and shows that ensembling reduces variance while finite N leaves a bias. The compute-dominance statement then explicitly assumes both bias B(N,t) and variance V(N,t) are nonincreasing in N, uses P to infinity, and prices compute as NEt. It does not cover diversity gains from heterogeneous models, parallel latency, memory limits, calibration, or cases where widening worsens bias or optimization.

anchors.section: Ensembling is not always compute optimal

key_findings.claim: The realistic-network evidence validates only a fitted lazy-kernel slope on one binary vision task, not the full dynamical theory.
key_findings.evidence: For animate-versus-inanimate CIFAR-5M, initial Wide-ResNet NTK curves are fit by b about 2 and an unexplained-task tail exponent a-1 about 0.15; inserting those same fitted exponents predicts a compute slope near -0.05, which visually follows the lazy-network frontier. The paper provides no uncertainty for either spectral fit or frontier exponent, no held-out task prediction, and no test of the DMFT correlation/response trajectories, finite-P law, or train-test gap on this network. Figures 1's CIFAR and WikiText cross-entropy curves motivate the phenomena but are not generated or fit by the MSE theory.

anchors.section: L. Kernel analysis of feature-learning networks

key_findings.claim: Feature learning is an observed failure of direct extrapolation from the model, not a mechanism explained by it.
key_findings.evidence: The student projection is frozen, so the theory is a lazy linear model by construction. Feature-learning ResNets trained for 64 epochs achieve a visibly steeper compute frontier than the predicted lazy slope. The after-kernel spectrum flattens and alignment changes, yet even a prediction built from the final kernel undershoots the observed loss improvement because the kernel keeps evolving. The conclusion correctly leaves a mechanistic theory of kernel evolution to future work; the later feature-learning competitor directly addresses this gap.

anchors.section: 5.1 role of feature learning and Figure 7c

key_findings.claim: The label-noise extension is not carried consistently through the stated closed equations.
key_findings.evidence: The main setup defines y(x) with an unrepresented sigma epsilon(x) component, but its displayed residual dynamics omit the corresponding forcing. Appendix A instead defines a noiseless population teacher and adds iid corrupted training labels; Equation 26 includes sigma epsilon in v1. The subsequent correlation closures on pages 14-16 set C1=R1 R1 C0 without the static sigma-squared covariance term and the power-law derivations analyze the noiseless loss. Thus the headline closure and exponents should be read as sigma=0 results, despite broader noise notation.

key_findings.claim: Several appendix equations are internally inconsistent enough that the derivation is not executable as printed.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 28 has unbound integration variables in the C0 and C1 lines. The saddle-point definition on page 18 inserts an extra lambda_k into R_2,4 despite its definitions on pages 5, 14, and 27 lacking that weight. Equation 107 drives v3 with v1 instead of v3, and Equation 109 repeats R3(omega) instead of R3(omega-prime). The discrete-time Equation 133 omits lambda_k in v2, the momentum transfer Equation 141 omits lambda_k, and the online-SGD Equation 142 has a plus update although Equation 143 and all residual-error dynamics require a minus. These look repairable, but without code they materially obstruct independent replication of the advertised extensions.

key_findings.claim: The power-law theory switches from an exact proportional limit to a less formal dimension-free approximation.
key_findings.evidence: The joint M,N,P proportional DMFT is presented as exact in its thermodynamic limit. For trace-class power-law kernels, however, Appendix G sends M to infinity first and replaces alpha and nu by finite P and N. Appendix J explicitly says the resulting expressions are not a formal proportional thermodynamic limit and that finite-system fluctuations remain, asserting that they decay rapidly enough based on prior work and simulations. This qualification matters because the headline exponents are derived in that non-proportional setting.

key_findings.claim: The compute proxy is coherent for the toy student but ambiguously transferred to the empirical networks.
key_findings.evidence: The theory has N trainable readout weights, so C=Nt is a reasonable fixed-cost proxy. In the empirical sections, N is described as channel width, while actual convolutional parameter/FLOP counts generally do not grow linearly with channel width; the paper does not state the conversion used in the compute plots. The proxy also omits depth, batch size, dataset generation, token or image cost, optimizer state, communication, and repeated-data cost, and the analytic optimization treats P as non-limiting.

anchors.section: Compute definition and empirical scaling motivation

key_findings.claim: The artifact is insufficient to reproduce either the numerical DMFT or the realistic-network figures.
key_findings.evidence: The PDF and current arXiv source contain no code or repository link. The source bundle has the TeX and 191 image assets, including many unused exploratory plots, but no scripts, configs, data manifests, checkpoints, seeds, or environment. Appendix M gives matrix iterations and a Fourier recipe, yet omits convergence tolerances, frequency grids, root/branch selection, and the parameters behind each plot. The CIFAR-5M and WikiText figures lack complete optimizer, batch, schedule, architecture, kernel-sampling, eigensolver, fit-window, repeat-count, and compute-accounting details.

anchors.section: M.2 Fourier recipe and compute appendix

key_findings.claim: The claimed larger-model training advantage is model- and parameterization-specific.
key_findings.evidence: Finite N changes the response-function pole structure and spreads each eigenmode over slower timescales, so increasing N accelerates this random-projection residual system. That does not by itself establish that arbitrary deeper or feature-learning networks train faster at matched steps: the projection distribution, normalization, learning-rate parameterization, optimizer, and evolving representation are held fixed or excluded. The empirical motivation adopts a width-consistent parameterization, a condition the headline should retain.

method.core_idea: Represent a finite lazy network as a Gaussian random projection of an infinite eigenfeature basis, train only a linear readout on squared loss, and average simultaneously over the projection and sampled dataset with dynamical mean-field theory.
method.mechanism: Residual teacher coefficients evolve under the product of a random feature Gram matrix and a sample covariance matrix. In large dimensions, correlation and response order parameters close; Fourier-domain transfer functions expose effective learning times for each spectral mode. Exact power-law feature and target tails then convert mode cutoffs into time, data, model, and compute exponents. Cross-realization correlations yield the data-reuse and ensemble decompositions.
assumptions: Training stays in a linearized or lazy regime with a frozen feature projection.
The finite network's features are modeled by an iid mean-zero, unit-variance random projection of complete infinite-width eigenfeatures.
Feature and sample matrix entries satisfy independence and central-limit or universality conditions; the primary path-integral derivation uses Gaussian entries.
M,N,P become large at fixed ratios for the exact proportional DMFT, or M is sent to infinity first for the dimension-free power-law approximation.
Optimization is squared-loss gradient flow unless using the stated discrete-time, momentum, or fresh-batch extensions.
Population eigenvalues and target power obey unbroken asymptotic power laws with exponents b and a.
The compute-optimal derivation approximates joint loss as additive time and model bottlenecks plus a constant and takes C=Nt.
The usual regime has a-1 no larger than 2b; the alternative easy-task exponent is treated as rare.
The headline bottleneck scalings are effectively noiseless despite sigma notation in the setup.
Self-averaging large-system order parameters describe the finite simulations and realistic lazy networks accurately enough.

techniques.role: Creates a controllable mismatch between an infinite spectral teacher and a finite projected student.
Averages projection and dataset disorder into closed correlation and response processes.
Re-derives the same processes by adding one feature, sample, or projected coordinate and clarifies universality assumptions.
Uses time-translation-invariant causal responses to solve transfer functions and extract early- and late-time behavior.
Maps spectral mode cutoffs to task-dependent resource exponents.
Obtains converged losses from the low-frequency response and correlation limits.
Interprets transfer functions as mixtures of exponential modes and recovers the Marchenko-Pastur law in an isotropic special case.
Separates dataset, initialization, and interaction variance for ensembling and bagging.
Fits initial and final Wide-ResNet kernel spectra and target-power tails on binary CIFAR-5M.
Provides a time-by-time numerical fixed-point recipe for correlations and responses.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic random features with a=1.5, b=1.25 and varied N, P, or t
evaluations.metric: Squared test loss and finite-resource residuals on log-log axes
evaluations.result: Finite simulations visually track DMFT curves, early corrections scale approximately as 1/N or 1/P, and late bottlenecks follow the predicted task-dependent powers.
evaluations.baseline: The paper's own large-system DMFT and asymptotic slopes; standard-deviation bands are shown but fit uncertainty is not reported.

evaluations.metric: Test loss versus steps for varied N or batch B
evaluations.result: The N bottleneck persists, while finite batch primarily adds variance rather than a B-dependent asymptotic floor in the plotted range.
evaluations.baseline: Online-SGD DMFT versus finite simulations; the printed update equation has the wrong sign.

evaluations.metric: Best loss envelope over N at fixed C=Nt
evaluations.result: The simulated envelope follows the predicted exponents -0.5, -0.4, and about -0.33.
evaluations.baseline: Optimization of the same synthetic model against the additive bottleneck asymptote.

evaluations.setting: Finite reused data P=128 or varied P in the synthetic model
evaluations.metric: Train loss, test loss, and their gap over time and width
evaluations.result: Wider models initially train faster, test loss saturates or becomes nonmonotone, and the train-test gap accumulates later for larger P.
evaluations.baseline: Exact DMFT gap expression and finite random realizations.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic ensembling and bagging with isotropic or power-law features
evaluations.metric: Infinite-time loss versus sample ratio and best loss versus C=NEt
evaluations.result: Ensembling suppresses variance and the theory recovers double-descent curves, but increasing N gives lower loss than increasing E under the stated monotonicity and compute assumptions.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-system DMFT and the infinite-width curve.

evaluations.setting: Wide ResNets on animate-versus-inanimate CIFAR-5M in the lazy regime
evaluations.metric: Initial NTK eigenvalue tail, unexplained target-power tail, and compute-optimal test loss
evaluations.result: Fitted b about 2 and a-1 about 0.15 imply a compute exponent near -0.05, visually agreeing with the lazy frontier.
evaluations.baseline: A slope predicted using exponents fitted on the same task; no uncertainty, held-out task, or alternative fit is supplied.

evaluations.setting: Feature-learning Wide ResNets on the same binary CIFAR-5M task for 64 epochs
evaluations.metric: Compute frontier, final-NTK spectrum, unexplained task power, kernel-target alignment, and kernel norm
evaluations.result: Feature-learning networks outperform the lazy slope; the final kernel flattens and aligns with the task, but a prediction from the after-kernel still underestimates the observed improvement.
evaluations.baseline: Initial-kernel random-feature theory and its predicted lazy frontier.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-5M residual CNN and WikiText transformer width sweeps shown in Figure 1
evaluations.metric: Cross-entropy train/test loss versus steps, tokens, width, and nominal compute
evaluations.result: The plots illustrate regular width/time scaling and data-reuse overfitting, but they are motivating observations rather than quantitative tests of the squared-loss DMFT.
evaluations.baseline: Empirical power-law guide curves with incomplete methods reporting.

limitations: The model is linear and lazy: it cannot explain feature discovery or evolving representations.
The exact proportional limit assumes large random matrices and substantial independence absent from a trained finite NTK.
Headline power-law exponents rely on exact unbroken spectral and target tails and mostly on the non-proportional approximation.
The compute-optimal law comes from an additive bottleneck ansatz and C=Nt, not measured end-to-end FLOPs or wall-clock cost.
CIFAR-5M provides only a same-task fitted lazy slope and no held-out prediction or confidence interval.
Feature-learning experiments visibly leave the regime described by the theory.
The empirical network methods are too sparse to reproduce architectures, kernels, fits, and compute accounting.
No official code, checkpoint, configuration, or executable numerical artifact is linked.
The source archive contains many unused plots but no scripts or data lineage.
Noise is introduced inconsistently and omitted from the displayed correlation closure.
Multiple appendix equations have missing variables, factors, frequency primes, or signs.
The online model assumes completely fresh independent batches and therefore cannot model finite-corpus streaming effects.
The ensembling dominance statement requires monotone bias and variance in width and ignores heterogeneous ensembles and systems constraints.
Cross-entropy language-model curves are outside the MSE teacher-student derivation.
There is no test across architectures, datasets, optimizers, learning-rate schedules, or realistic language-model scales.
failure_modes: Feature learning changes the kernel spectrum or target alignment, invalidating frozen-projection transfer functions.
Finite models have structured, dependent NTK features rather than iid Gaussian projections.
Broken, curved, finite-rank, or multi-regime spectra make a single a,b forecast unstable.
Label noise contributes covariance terms and early-stopping tradeoffs absent from the noiseless bottleneck formula.
Cross-entropy or other nonlinear losses do not share the linear residual dynamics.
Learning-rate decay, Adam, momentum scaling, regularization, or batch schedules alter time and compute exponents.
Repeated examples, curriculum, augmentation, or distribution drift violate both iid offline and fresh-batch online assumptions.
A finite P,N system near interpolation fails to self-average and exhibits large seed-dependent deviations.
Treating channel width as parameter count gives the wrong compute exponent for convolutional or transformer architectures.
A wider model can have optimization instability, worse conditioning, or nonmonotone bias, defeating the ensemble comparison.
Summing separate asymptotic bottlenecks misses interactions and crossovers in joint finite-resource regimes.
Numerical implementations following the printed appendix literally produce incorrect dynamics because of missing lambda factors or the SGD sign error.
reusable_insights: Measure learning dynamics per spectral mode, not only final aggregate loss; finite resources change both learnability and timescale distributions.
Separate early universal 1/N or 1/P corrections from late task-dependent exponents when using small models as scaling proxies.
Treat fitted kernel spectra as a falsifiable forecast: estimate a and b on one task or scale, preregister a loss slope, and test it on held-out widths and budgets.
Use a frozen-feature model as a null baseline, then quantify the residual gain attributable to kernel evolution.
Decompose ensemble gains into bias, initialization variance, dataset variance, and their interaction before comparing ensemble count with width.
Report both proportional-limit and dimension-free assumptions beside every claimed exponent.
Validate additive compute laws against the exact joint finite-resource surface rather than only its one-axis asymptotes.
Define compute with measured FLOPs, tokens or samples, memory, and communication; do not silently substitute architectural width.
Carry label noise through every effective process and covariance equation, and verify the sigma=0 reduction separately.
Publish executable equation tests for limiting cases such as infinite data, infinite width, isotropic Marchenko-Pastur spectra, and online sign conventions.
Compare power laws with broken laws and plateaus and report fit windows, uncertainty, and sensitivity to rank truncation.
Use after-kernel analysis cautiously: a kernel measured at the end cannot explain a trajectory if it continues evolving over the fitted interval.
open_questions: Can the same joint time-data-width DMFT be solved for an evolving feature map rather than a frozen projection?
Which aspects of the response-function theory survive cross-entropy, softmax, and modern adaptive optimizers?
Do spectral exponents estimated at small width or early time forecast held-out large-scale loss without refitting?
How should label noise and target misspecification modify the correlation closure and compute-optimal stopping rule?
Can one prove a dimension-free finite-N,P approximation with explicit error rates for the power-law regime used in the headline results?
When does the joint loss actually decompose into additive time, model, and data terms, and what are the leading interaction terms?
How do broken spectra, finite rank, multiple task subspaces, and changing data mixtures alter the bottleneck phase diagram?
Can measured hardware compute and communication costs reverse the predicted allocation between width, training time, and ensembling?
Does ensemble diversity from architecture, data order, or objectives reduce bias as well as variance?
Can the discrete-time, momentum, and online-SGD appendices be corrected and validated against a released reference implementation?
What empirical protocol distinguishes genuine spectral-mechanism prediction from fitting the same task's spectrum and loss slope?
Can response and correlation functions be estimated directly from network checkpoints to test the DMFT beyond aggregate loss curves?

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Earlier spectral-resolution theory for data and model scaling
competitive_landscape.difference: Bahri et al. organize fixed-kernel and random-feature learning into variance- and resolution-limited regimes and connect task smoothness to exponents. The reviewed paper adds explicit training dynamics, data reuse, ensembling, and asymmetric time-versus-width compute allocation, while inheriting a fixed-feature spectral explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest earlier solvable random-feature scaling model
competitive_landscape.difference: Maloney, Roberts, and Sully derive parameter/data power laws, plateaus, and feature-sample duality at convergence. The reviewed paper adds gradient-descent time, response functions, repeated-data gaps, and compute allocation, but uses another idealized Gaussian random-feature construction.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Empirical compute-optimal scaling target motivating the theory
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoffmann et al. fit transformer loss as separate parameter and token powers using large language-model sweeps and recommend balancing the two resources. The reviewed paper offers a spectral random-feature mechanism for an asymmetric width-time balance, but its C=Nt proxy and MSE model do not reproduce the Chinchilla experimental setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling and Renormalization in High-Dimensional Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Atanasov et al. use free probability to derive generalization and bias-variance formulas for structured covariates, ridge, and finite features. The reviewed paper is more explicitly dynamical and treats data reuse and ensembles, but is narrower in regularization and empirical covariance structure.

competitive_landscape.title: 4+3 Phases of Compute-Optimal Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct rigorous one-pass random-feature compute-scaling competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: Paquette et al. derive a detailed phase diagram whose boundaries depend on capacity, optimizer noise, and feature embedding. The reviewed paper supplies reusable-data gradient-flow dynamics and train-test-gap buildup, while its compact m=min(a-1,2b) compute law omits several optimizer-noise phases identified by the later analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Scaling Laws from Large-N Field Theory: Solvable Model beyond the Ridgeless Limit
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous large-N equilibrium field theory with finite ridge
competitive_landscape.difference: This work extends the Maloney random-feature model to arbitrary ridge, derives corrected optimal-loss laws, and exposes feature-sample diagram duality, but assumes convergence and provides no training dynamics. The reviewed paper covers time, early stopping, and data reuse but does not analyze arbitrary regularization.

competitive_landscape.title: Dimension-free deterministic equivalents and scaling laws for random feature regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct later theory for finite random-feature regression without proportional asymptotics
competitive_landscape.difference: Defilippis et al. establish dimension-free deterministic equivalents and sharp excess-risk rates under source and capacity assumptions, directly strengthening the mathematical status of the regime that the reviewed paper calls non-formal. They focus on regression risk rather than the reviewed paper's transient DMFT, overfitting buildup, and ensemble dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest direct successor beyond the frozen random-feature regime
competitive_landscape.difference: Atanasov et al. make the feature projection trainable, derive hard/easy task regimes where feature learning changes time and compute exponents, and test MLP, CNN, and language settings. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's acknowledged failure on feature-learning CIFAR curves, though still uses a projected solvable model and restricted loss dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Collapse Reveals Universal Dynamics in Compute-Optimally Trained Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later empirically anchored account of compute-optimal loss dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. demonstrate normalized loss-curve collapse across architectures, datasets, next-token transformers, and learning-rate schedules and model its SGD-noise origin. The reviewed paper instead predicts spectral resource bottlenecks in a random-feature MSE model and does not cover schedule-dependent collapse.

competitive_landscape.title: Dimension-adapted Momentum Outscales SGD
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later optimizer-based competitor on power-law random features
competitive_landscape.difference: Ferbach et al. show that dimension-adapted Nesterov momentum can improve training and compute exponents while ordinary momentum preserves SGD exponents. This demonstrates that exponent changes need not come from data spectra or feature evolution alone and exposes how incomplete the reviewed paper's brief momentum extension is.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current direct successor for time-dependent power-law random-feature regression
competitive_landscape.difference: The 2026 work quantitatively treats eigenmode dynamics, weight decay, Langevin noise, generalization, and early stopping in a closely related setting. It postdates the reviewed paper and offers a controlled benchmark for its noisy and regularized extensions, whereas the reviewed work uniquely foregrounds the joint projection-and-dataset DMFT and ensemble decomposition.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a solvable dynamical model that simultaneously explains time, data, model, and compute power laws, faster training at larger width, universal early and task-dependent late finite-resource corrections, gradual data-reuse overfitting, and why widening beats ensembling.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact proportional-limit response closure, Fourier transfer functions, recovery of known static limits, power-law asymptotics, synthetic DMFT comparisons, cross-system ensemble calculation, and one realistic lazy-NTK fit substantiate a meaningful theoretical advance over final-loss-only models.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The genuinely novel core is the joint transient DMFT over both random projection and sampled data, especially the response-function view of finite-width/data timescales and the cross-system variance decomposition. The headline neural-scaling interpretation is narrower: exponents are inherited from imposed spectral tails, compute optimality uses an additive C=Nt proxy, and the only realistic match fits spectrum and loss on the same binary CIFAR task. Feature learning visibly defeats the model and is handled by later direct successors. Noise is not closed consistently, several printed extension equations are wrong, and no code exists. A corrected artifact would retain the noiseless continuous-time core, repair and test the appendix equations, qualify the non-proportional limit, release all experiment and DMFT code, and validate preregistered held-out forecasts.

reviewer_notes: Read all 38 pages of arXiv:2402.01092v4, including every main-text plot, all 12 numbered figures and their panels, all derivations in Appendices A-N, the path-integral and cavity arguments, final-value asymptotics, ensemble/bagging algebra, discrete-time/momentum/online extensions, realistic NTK appendix, and numerical recipes. Audited the complete current arXiv source bundle (195 files: TeX/style/bibliography plus 191 image assets, many unused) and found no code, configuration, checkpoint, or repository link. Checked the printed equations against the TeX source; the unbound variables, extra or missing lambda factors, repeated frequency argument, v1/v3 substitution, missing momentum-mode factor, and online-SGD sign are source-level issues rather than text-extraction artifacts. Checked 11 primary competitors and successors through 2026-08-23, including the direct feature-learning, dimension-free, optimizer, and 2026 dynamical random-feature follow-ups.
